claims.claim: Keeley says a single first-person sentence near the end of an otherwise third-person Wolfe book asks readers to reconsider everything already read.
claims.quote: asks readers to reconsider everything that they’ve already read

claims.claim: Kelly says the narrator of The Fifth Head of Cerberus describes his surroundings at face value and leaves understanding to the reader.
claims.source: Mark R. Kelly, Views from Crestmont Drive, 3 July 2014
claims.quote: describes his surroundings at face value, leaving it up to the reader

claims.claim: Kelly says a Wolfe story carries an underlying real story that the point-of-view character does not necessarily understand and that Wolfe expects the reader to deduce.
claims.source: Mark R. Kelly, Views from Crestmont Drive, 3 July 2014
claims.quote: which Wolfe counts on the reader to being able to deduce

claims.claim: Kelly says the fact that the narrator's large house is a brothel emerges in the course of the narration rather than being stated.
claims.source: Mark R. Kelly, Views from Crestmont Drive, 3 July 2014
claims.quote: It develops that this large house is a brothel.

claims.claim: Kelly, summarising Joan Gordon's 1986 Starmont study, says the novella's theme is underscored by small details in the text such as the house's address.
claims.source: Mark R. Kelly, Views from Crestmont Drive, 3 July 2014, relaying Joan Gordon's 1986 Starmont House study of Wolfe
claims.quote: underscored by small details in the text

claims.feature: other: precision as a constant of the prose
claims.claim: Kelly says it is difficult to find a paragraph anywhere in Wolfe that is not both precise and poetic.
claims.source: Mark R. Kelly, Views from Crestmont Drive, 3 July 2014

claims.claim: Macdonald says the things Severian knows that the reader does not are left unexplained because they are the mysteries of his trade.
claims.quote: are not explained because they are the mysteries of his trade

claims.claim: Macdonald says Wolfe's new vocabulary is mainly nouns that sound as if made from a familiar root by changing a vowel or suffix.
claims.quote: His new vocabulary (mainly nouns) sounds as if it was altered

claims.claim: Macdonald says the meaning of Wolfe's strange words is fairly obvious from context.
claims.quote: Their meaning is fairly obvious in the context

claims.claim: Macdonald says Wolfe also changes the meaning of real words, giving destrier as her example.
claims.quote: He also changes the meaning of real words, like destrier

claims.claim: Macdonald says Wolfe's frame invites the reader to think about these stories as histories, reports, assessments and commentaries rather than only as story.
claims.quote: we also think about these stories as histories, reports, assessments, commentaries
claims.page: body, paragraph on the appended note about invented words

claims.claim: Macdonald says the torture is reported from a very clinical viewpoint.
claims.quote: we’re told about the event from a very clinical viewpoint
claims.page: body, paragraph on the torture scenes

claims.claim: Macdonald says the narration withholds screams, bleeding flesh and details of pain from the torture scenes, so the reader feels no immediate horrified empathy.
claims.quote: we aren’t told anything about screams, bleeding flesh, details of pain
claims.page: body, paragraph on the torture scenes

claims.claim: Macdonald says Wolfe casts casual asides into the reader's path just when attention is expected elsewhere.
claims.quote: casting casual asides down in our path
claims.page: body, paragraph on gaps in knowledge

claims.claim: A MetaFilter reader reports that in Shadow of the Torturer the narrator meets a blind man and never mentions that he is blind.
claims.quote: encounters a blind man but never mentions he is blind

verdicts.trueWording: a single sentence in the first person near the very end of a book otherwise in the third person asks readers to reconsider everything that they've already read
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of reactormag.com fetched directly (curl, 200). Sentence present word for word in the paragraph after the Fifth Head of Cerberus opening-line discussion. Byline 'By Matthew Keeley | Published on November 9, 2017' confirmed on page. Every limb (single sentence, first person, near the very end, otherwise third person, reconsider everything already read) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: the main character describes his surroundings at face value, leaving it up to the reader to understand, or not
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (curl -k; the host's TLS chain fails verification, content served 200 and matches the live article, byline 'Posted on Thursday 3 July 2014 by Mark R. Kelly'). Quote verbatim. Page says 'the main character'; the article has already established that character as the first-person narrator of The Fifth Head of Cerberus.

verdicts.trueWording: there is an *underlying* story, a 'real' story, that the pov character does not necessarily understand, but which Wolfe counts on the reader to being able to deduce
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (including the page's own ungrammatical 'to being able to deduce'). Both limbs -- pov character does not necessarily understand; Wolfe counts on the reader to deduce -- are on the page, and the page generalises it to 'most if not all of his works'.

verdicts.trueWording: It develops that this large house is a brothel.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Kelly's plot summary. The house is the narrator's: the preceding sentence has the narrator living 'with his brother David in a big house in the city of Port-Mimizon'. The limb 'emerges in the course of the narration rather than being stated' is carried by 'It develops that', reinforced by the next paragraph ('describes his surroundings at face value, leaving it up to the reader').

verdicts.trueWording: Gordon goes on to explain how the novella's theme of denying human individuality is underscored by small details in the text: the address of the house at 666
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the house-address example ('the address of the house at 666...') is on the page. Attribution limbs confirmed: 'Joan Gordon, author of a thin Starmont Press paperback about Gene Wolfe's works, published way back in 1986'. Minor metadata drift only: the claim's source line says 'Starmont House'; Kelly writes 'Starmont Press'.

verdicts.trueWording: It is difficult to find a paragraph in any of Wolfe's works that is not both precise and poetic.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; 'in any of Wolfe's works' supports the claim's 'anywhere in Wolfe'. Sentence sits immediately before the sample paragraph Kelly quotes at random, as the claim's page hint says.

verdicts.trueWording: the things that Severian knows about that we don't are not explained because they are the mysteries of his trade
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched directly (katemacdonald.net, curl 200; title 'Gene Wolfe's The Shadow of the Torturer - Kate Macdonald', 'Published January 9, 2017'). Quote verbatim; every limb on the page, which continues 'and we the readers are not privy to these'.

verdicts.trueWording: His new vocabulary (mainly nouns) sounds as if it was altered by changing a vowel or suffix to make new words from a familiar root.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim and the rest of the sentence supplies the claim's remaining limbs (familiar root, vowel or suffix).

verdicts.trueWording: Their meaning is fairly obvious in the context
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, immediately after Macdonald's sample list (cataphract, optimate, armigette, fuligin, etc.), so 'Wolfe's strange words' is the correct referent.

verdicts.trueWording: He also changes the meaning of real words, like destrier, which in his world isn't a horse
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; destrier is given as the example exactly as the claim states.

verdicts.trueWording: So we don't just read 'story', we also think about these stories as histories, reports, assessments, commentaries
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The 'frame' limb is supported by the same paragraph: 'For this purportedly post-historic frame narrative Wolfe adds a note at the end... inviting the reader to think about these stories as being the narratives and records of history that have not happened yet.' 'rather than only as story' is the page's own 'we don't just read story'.

verdicts.trueWording: Instead, we're told about the event from a very clinical viewpoint, and also an artist's perspective.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. 'The event' is the torture scene -- the preceding sentence names 'a torture scene'. The claim omits, but does not contradict, the page's added 'and also an artist's perspective'.

verdicts.trueWording: Because we aren't told anything about screams, bleeding flesh, details of pain... we don't feel immediate horrified empathy
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and the consequence limb ('so the reader feels no immediate horrified empathy') is the same sentence's main clause.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe is an expert distracter of attention, of casting casual asides down in our path just as we expect to be focusing on something else
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the 'just when attention is expected elsewhere' limb is the page's 'just as we expect to be focusing on something else'.

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator encounters a blind man but never mentions he is blind
verdicts.note: Raw MetaFilter thread 149475 fetched directly (curl 200). Quote verbatim inside the comment attributed on-page to 'posted by straight at 9:00 AM on May 8, 2015'; the same comment names 'Shadow of the Torturer' as the book. All limbs confirmed.
